note: 24 fresh novel questions about Frankenstein, written for this test, not from any benchmark. Each requires combining or applying book knowledge, not single-sentence recall. Grading rule: an answer is correct only if it contains ALL listed key facts (in meaning, not exact wording).

questions.expected: The creature wants revenge on Victor by destroying the people Victor loves, and framing Justine turns Victor's own household and the law against an innocent. The planted locket is the evidence that convicts her, so Victor watches an innocent servant he cares for be executed for a crime the creature committed.
key_facts: the creature wants revenge on Victor by hurting those Victor loves
the locket is planted as evidence that convicts Justine
an innocent person is executed for the creature's crime
questions.question: Why does the creature plant William's locket in Justine Moritz's pocket instead of simply leaving after killing William?

questions.expected: From the De Laceys he learns language, human affection and kindness, and also that humans judge him by his appearance: when he finally approaches the blind old man kindly and then Felix returns, Felix beats him and drives him off. That teaches him humans will never accept him, so he stops seeking human acceptance and turns to demanding a companion from Victor instead.
key_facts: he learns language and human affection from the De Laceys
Felix beats and drives him off when he approaches them
he concludes humans will never accept him and turns to demanding a companion from Victor
questions.question: What does the creature learn from watching the De Lacey family that changes how he approaches Victor?

questions.expected: Victor fears the female may be more evil than the male, that she may refuse him, and that the two could have children and spread a race of devils over the earth. He also realises the creature may use her to threaten or torment mankind. The fear of what the pair could become outweighs his promise.
key_facts: he fears the pair could have children and spread a race of devils
he fears the female may be more evil or refuse the creature
the fear outweighs his promise to the creature
questions.question: Why does Victor destroy the female creature after he has already built most of her?

questions.expected: Walton, like Victor, is an ambitious young man pursuing a grand and dangerous goal in isolation, seeking glory and knowledge, and lacking a friend. Victor tells Walton his story as a warning, and Walton is the one who hears it and can still choose differently. The mirror is what lets Walton turn back when his crew demands it, where Victor could not stop himself.
key_facts: Walton is ambitious, isolated and seeking glory like Victor
Victor tells his story to Walton as a warning
Walton turns back where Victor could not stop
questions.question: In what ways does Walton's situation mirror Victor's, and why does that matter to the story?

questions.expected: He has already tried to be accepted by humans and been beaten, shot and driven away, most clearly at the De Laceys' cottage and when he saved the drowning girl. He has concluded no human will ever accept him because of his appearance, so only a being like himself could ever be his companion.
key_facts: he has already been rejected and attacked by humans
he concludes no human will accept him because of his appearance
only a being like himself could be his companion
questions.question: Why does the creature ask Victor for a companion of his own kind rather than asking to be accepted by humans?

questions.expected: In Paradise Lost he finds both Adam and Satan and sees himself in both: like Adam he was created and then abandoned by his creator, and like Satan he is cast out, envied and turned to bitterness. The book gives him the language to frame his own story as a created being wronged by his maker.
key_facts: he identifies with Adam, created then abandoned by his creator
he identifies with Satan, cast out and turned bitter
the book gives him a frame for his own story
questions.question: Why is the creature's reading of Paradise Lost important to how he understands himself?

questions.expected: Victor knows the creature did it but knows no one would believe him, a tale of an eight-foot creature would sound like madness, and telling the truth would expose his own crime of creating the creature. His shame and fear of disbelief keep him silent, and his silence lets an innocent woman hang.
key_facts: he knows no one would believe a story about the creature
telling the truth would expose his own act of creation
his silence lets an innocent woman be executed
questions.question: Why does Victor stay silent at Justine's trial when he knows the creature killed William?

questions.expected: The creature destroys, one by one, everyone Victor loves: William first, then Justine through the framing, then Henry Clerval in Ireland, then Elizabeth on her wedding night, and Victor's father dies of grief after it. Elizabeth is the last and most intimate, the creature's threat to be with Victor on his wedding night was aimed at her all along, and her death leaves Victor with nothing left to lose.
key_facts: the creature kills everyone Victor loves, one by one
Elizabeth's death fulfils the wedding-night threat
her death leaves Victor with nothing left to lose
questions.question: How does Elizabeth's murder complete the pattern of the creature's revenge on Victor?

questions.expected: Safie is a Turkish woman who arrives at the De Lacey cottage speaking no French, so Felix teaches her the language with books and lessons. The creature watches and listens through the cottage wall and learns language the same way she does, at the same pace, which is how he gains speech and then reading.
key_facts: Felix teaches Safie French because she does not speak it
the creature learns by listening to those lessons through the wall
that is how he gains language and then reading
questions.question: What role does Safie play in the creature's education, and why does he learn alongside her?

questions.expected: He needs a remote, isolated place where no one will see or interrupt his work, far from people and from the creature's watch. Orkney is desolate and lonely, which suits secret work, and it also puts distance between him and his family while he does something he dreads.
key_facts: he needs isolation so no one sees or interrupts the work
Orkney is remote and desolate
the secrecy is because he dreads the work
questions.question: Why does Victor go to the Orkney Islands to build the female creature?

questions.expected: Toward the De Laceys he is secretly benevolent: he brings them firewood, clears snow, leaves food, and does them good without reward, because they show him kindness and affection from a distance. Toward Victor's family he is vengeful and destructive because Victor abandoned and rejected him. The contrast shows he was not born evil; he became vengeful after being rejected.
key_facts: he secretly helps the De Laceys with firewood and food
he destroys Victor's family in revenge for being abandoned
the contrast shows he became vengeful after rejection, not born evil
questions.question: How does the creature's behaviour toward the De Lacey family differ from his behaviour toward Victor's family, and what does that show?

questions.expected: Alphonse thinks Victor's distress is ordinary grief over William, and later suspects it is love-sickness or anxiety about Elizabeth, and he tries to comfort him with talk of marriage and the future. He never guesses the real cause, that Victor created the creature and knows it killed William, so his well-meant comfort misses the truth entirely.
key_facts: Alphonse thinks the distress is grief over William or love for Elizabeth
he tries to comfort Victor with talk of marriage and the future
he never guesses Victor created the creature
questions.question: What does Victor's father Alphonse misunderstand about Victor's distress after William's death?

questions.expected: The creature flees north to the desolate Arctic and Victor follows, because the ice and emptiness match the creature's isolation and Victor's own desolation. It is also where Walton's ship is trapped, so the chase ends where the frame story began, and the Arctic is the one place with no people left for the creature to harm or Victor to lose.
key_facts: the Arctic's desolation matches the creature's isolation and Victor's desolation
it is where Walton's ship is trapped, closing the frame
it is a place with no people left to harm or lose
questions.question: Why does the final chase between Victor and the creature take place in the Arctic, and what does the setting mean?

questions.expected: Walton's letters to his sister Margaret open and close the novel, Victor tells his life to Walton, and the creature tells his life to Victor, so the story is nested three deep. Each teller is unreliable in his own way and each one passes the tale to a listener who judges it, which keeps the reader at a distance and makes the question of who is to blame stay open.
key_facts: Walton's letters frame the novel and Victor's story is told inside them
the creature's story is nested inside Victor's story
the nesting keeps the question of blame open
questions.question: How does Mary Shelley use Walton's letters as a frame, and what does the nesting of stories do?

questions.expected: He sees a girl drowning in a stream and pulls her out, acting from the benevolence he learned with the De Laceys, and her companion, a man, shoots him in the shoulder for seizing her. He takes from it the final proof that humans repay his good deeds with violence and that his appearance alone condemns him, which hardens him into revenge.
key_facts: he saves a drowning girl out of benevolence
her companion shoots him for seizing her
he takes it as proof humans repay good with violence
questions.question: Why does the creature save a drowning girl and then get shot for it, and what does he take from that?

questions.expected: Victor brings the creature to life on a dreary night of November, at one in the morning, in the rain, after two years of work. The dark, cold, dead hour matches the unnaturalness of the act and the horror of what he has made, and the moment his eyes open and the creature breathes, Victor is seized with disgust and flees, so the creature's first experience of life is abandonment in the dark.
key_facts: it happens on a dreary November night at one in the morning
the dark dead hour matches the unnaturalness of the act
Victor flees at once, so the creature's first experience is abandonment
questions.question: Why is the timing of the creature's animation, a dreary night in November at one in the morning, significant?

questions.expected: Justine is innocent but her confessor pressures her, telling her that confessing will save her soul and that the evidence, the locket found in her pocket, condemns her anyway. She confesses falsely because she is frightened, isolated and persuaded that a false confession is her only hope of mercy, and the confession seals her execution.
key_facts: her confessor pressures her to confess to save her soul
the planted locket is treated as proof against her
the false confession seals her execution
questions.question: Why does Justine confess to a murder she did not commit?

questions.expected: The creature argues his case with eloquence, promises that if he has a companion he will leave Europe and live with her in the deserts of South America where no human will ever see them, and appeals to Victor's pity and sense of duty as his creator. Victor is moved by the creature's suffering and afraid of what he will do if refused, so he promises, and only later destroys her when the fear of a new race outweighs the promise.
key_facts: the creature promises to leave Europe and live in the wilderness with a companion
Victor is moved by pity and by fear of refusal
he promises, then later breaks the promise
questions.question: Why does Victor agree to create a female creature at all, after refusing at first?

questions.expected: The creature means he will kill Elizabeth on Victor's wedding night, taking the person Victor loves most on the night he is happiest. Victor misunderstands because he assumes the threat is aimed at himself, he thinks the creature will kill him, so he spends the wedding night watching for his own death and leaves Elizabeth alone, which lets the creature reach her.
key_facts: the threat is aimed at Elizabeth, not Victor
Victor assumes the creature will kill him
he leaves Elizabeth alone, letting the creature reach her
questions.question: What does the creature mean when he says he will be with Victor on his wedding night, and why does Victor misunderstand it?

questions.expected: He first sees his own reflection in a pool of water and is horrified, and he later finds Victor's journal in the pocket of a coat he took, which describes the creature's creation and Victor's disgust at his appearance. Learning he is hideous explains why everyone flees him, and it turns his confusion into a settled conviction that he can never be loved.
key_facts: he sees his reflection in a pool and is horrified
Victor's journal describes his creation and Victor's disgust
it convinces him he can never be loved
questions.question: How does the creature learn what he looks like, and what effect does that knowledge have on him?

questions.expected: After the creature comes alive Victor is seized with horror and disgust, flees his workshop, and collapses into a nervous fever that lasts months, nursed by Henry Clerval. The illness is the physical form of his guilt and terror: he has done what he set out to do and cannot bear what he made, and the fever keeps him from having to face it.
key_facts: he collapses into a nervous fever lasting months after the creation
Henry Clerval nurses him through it
the illness is guilt and horror at what he made
questions.question: Why does Victor fall into a months-long nervous fever after creating the creature?

questions.expected: Clerval is Victor's closest friend from childhood, a healthy, humanist foil to Victor's obsessive science, who nurses Victor through his fever and restores him to life and study. The creature murders him in Ireland and leaves the body where Victor will find it, which breaks Victor completely, because Clerval is the one person who kept Victor human, and his death is the creature's revenge reaching Victor's dearest friend.
key_facts: Clerval is Victor's closest friend and a foil to his obsessive science
Clerval nurses Victor through his fever
his murder breaks Victor because Clerval kept him human
questions.question: What is Henry Clerval's role in the story, and why does his murder matter more than a stranger's death would?

questions.expected: Walton's crew, trapped in the ice and facing death, demand to turn back, and Walton, having heard Victor's whole story as a warning against sacrificing everything for a grand ambition, agrees. He chooses the lives of his men and his own return over the glory of reaching the pole, which is the choice Victor never made, and it is the one way Walton proves he learned from Victor's tale.
key_facts: his crew demands to turn back from the ice
Victor's story warned him against sacrificing everything for ambition
he chooses his men's lives over the glory of the pole
questions.question: Why does Walton decide to turn his ship back instead of pushing on to the North Pole?

questions.expected: Speaking over Victor's dead body, the creature says he was once benevolent and became miserable and vengeful only after being rejected and denied sympathy, that his crimes have made him hate himself, and that he will now end his own life by fire. He asks Walton to understand that he suffered as much as he made others suffer, which reframes him from a monster into a being ruined by his creator's abandonment.
key_facts: he says he was once benevolent and became vengeful only after rejection
he says his crimes made him hate himself
he says he will end his own life by fire
questions.question: How does the creature's final speech to Walton change how we judge him?
